item.title: Boston Scientific Exposes 117,000 Records Following Voice Phishing Attack
item.description:
Boston Scientific Exposes 117,000 Records Following Voice Phishing Attack

Boston Scientific, a Massachusetts-based medical device manufacturer, is sending data breach notices to individuals after a cyberattack exposed personal and medical information belonging to 117,789 people in the United States. The incident marks the second cybersecurity event for the company this year.

🔍 Overview

The attack exposed cloud-based applications and cloud-hosted data between May 7 and May 1, 2025. Boston Scientific became aware of the unauthorized access on May 12. A subsequent investigation determined that a data breach occurred on November 5. The exposed information included personal details and medical information for individuals in multiple U.S. states.

🧩 How it works

According to notification samples shared with U.S. authorities, the hacker gained access to the company’s cloud infrastructure using social engineering in a voice phishing (vishing) attack.

⚙️ Key details

  • Data Exposed: Personal details and medical information.
  • Data Not Exposed: The notification specifies that patient medical records, data from remote monitoring systems, connected medical devices, and clinical case management or workflow applications were not exposed.
  • Scope: The incident impacted 117,789 individuals according to the Texas Attorney General breach portal.
  • Business Impact: The company stated there was no disruption to manufacturing, ordering, distribution, or service to patients and healthcare providers, and no impact on operations, performance, remote monitoring, or the safety of its products.

📊 Incident Comparison

This breach is distinct from a previous cyberattack disclosed on August 25, which caused network outages and global operational disruptions. A Boston Scientific spokesperson confirmed the most recent incident is unrelated to the August 2026 intrusion; a CrowdStrike investigation into that earlier attack found no evidence that attackers compromised cloud applications.

💡 Why it matters

As one of the world’s largest medical device manufacturers with more than 59,000 employees, 13 manufacturing facilities, and a presence in 127 countries, Boston Scientific’s data security is critical. The company contained the incident, investigated with outside cybersecurity experts, and notified law enforcement. However, the company is not offering free credit monitoring and instead recommends impacted individuals use free credit reports, place fraud alerts, and consider credit freezes.

#databreach #cybersecurity #medicaldevices #vishing #BostonScientific

Source: New Boston Scientific data breach exposes personal, medical info

item.title: pCloud Pass users report unauthorized device connections following cyberattack
item.description:
pCloud Pass users report unauthorized device connections following cyberattack

The pCloud Pass password manager was recently targeted by a cyberattack, resulting in users reporting that unknown devices had connected to their accounts, some with two-factor authentication (2FA) enabled. The attack was contained by the pCloud team, though a small number of user email addresses were exposed.

🔍 Overview

According to pCloud, a cyberattack targeting pCloud Pass occurred and was promptly contained. The company stated that a small number of pCloud Pass user email addresses were exposed and that login attempts were made. The system automatically sent notifications to each of these affected addresses.

⚙️ Key details

  • Users reported receiving notifications warning that an unfamiliar device named “pd” connected to their account from IP address 45.131.244.7 in Luxembourg.
  • The IP address is reportedly part of pCloud’s own infrastructure.
  • Notifications were received by customers who had 2FA enabled.
  • Some users who never used the password manager, including those with deleted storage accounts, also received the alerts.
  • PCloud stated the attack was isolated to the password manager, and cloud storage services were not affected.
  • Passwords, notes, and other information stored in pCloud Pass are encrypted on customer devices and were not compromised.
  • It is unknown whether encrypted password vaults were accessed or stolen during the attack.
  • A reader noted that the “Open settings” link in the email notifications pointed to passqa1.pcloud.com, a QA environment, rather than the production site.

💡 Why it matters

Threat actors who obtain encrypted password vaults can attempt to crack them offline, bypassing the service’s login rate limits and two-factor authentication protections. This risk was demonstrated in the 2022 LastPass breach, where stolen encrypted password vaults were linked to cryptocurrency thefts after attackers cracked weak or reused master passwords.

🛡️ Security advice

  • pCloud is warning customers to watch for phishing attacks.
  • The company states it will never ask for master passwords or recovery words over email, phone, or chat.
  • PCloud noted that advancements in artificial intelligence are accelerating the discovery of software vulnerabilities, though it did not state that this specific attack was AI-powered.

#pCloud #PasswordManager #Cybersecurity #DataBreach #2FA

Source: pCloud confirms password manager hack after suspicious login alerts

item.title: Q-Dir and DesktopOK Installers Compromised with Python-Based Malware
item.description:
Q-Dir and DesktopOK Installers Compromised with Python-Based Malware

Official distribution channels for the popular Windows utilities Q-Dir and DesktopOK were compromised to deliver trojanized installers containing Python-based remote access malware, according to a report from AhnLab’s Security Intelligence Center (ASEC).

🧩 Malware Capabilities

The malicious installers fetch a Python Remote Access Trojan (RAT) that registers a scheduled task to persist on infected devices. The malware supports the following capabilities:

  • Shell command and Python code execution
  • File transfer
  • Screenshot capture
  • System information collection, including a list of active security products

📊 Impacted Versions

ASEC confirmed that the compromise affected both new downloads and updates for existing installations. Not all listed versions were infected. The following release versions are impacted:

Product Affected Versions
Q-Dir 12.83.0.0, 12.84.0.0, 12.85.0.0
DesktopOK 12.82.0.0, 12.85.0.0

🕵️ Security Detection Evasion

The malware collects a list of 1,206 processes matching various antivirus and endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools to relay to the command and control server. This allows operators to plan their next actions without getting detected. The targeted security products include:

  • AhnLab V3
  • CrowdStrike Falcon
  • SentinelOne
  • rend Micro
  • Avast
  • McAfee
  • ESET
  • Symantec
  • Kaspersky
  • Bitdefender
  • Sophos
  • Fortinet
  • Elastic Security
  • Malwarebytes
  • FireEye

🛡️ Remediation and Verification

AhnLab researchers provided SHA-256 hashes to help users distinguish legitimate installers from malicious ones. Users are advised to check their downloads against the SHA-256 published on the official download page.

Removing a trojanized version of Q-Dir or DesktopOK does not ensure the elimination of the Python RAT. Users who recently installed or updated these tools should treat their system as potentially compromised and check for:

  • Suspicious Python execution environments
  • Scheduled tasks
  • Traces of external network communication

The trojanized versions are digitally signed using a certificate issued to the legitimate developer, Nenad Hrg, who distributes the tools through the SoftwareOK website. ASEC could not determine how the installers were replaced or the timeframe during which the malicious versions were distributed.

#WindowsSecurity #SupplyChainAttack #Trojan #QDir #DesktopOK #Cybersecurity

Source: Q-Dir and DesktopOK Windows utilities compromised to push Python RAT

item.title: Zero-Day SQL Injection Enables Command Execution in Cacti Monitoring Platform
item.description:
Zero-Day SQL Injection Enables Command Execution in Cacti Monitoring Platform

A zero‑day SQL injection vulnerability in the open‑source network monitoring tool Cacti was publicly disclosed, accompanied by a proof‑of‑concept exploit that lets unauthenticated attackers execute commands on vulnerable servers.

🔍 Overview

  • The vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to inject SQL into the Cacti database.
  • It can modify the commands executed by Cacti’s real‑time poller.
  • The exploit requires the Cacti guest account to be enabled.

🧩 How it Works

  • Attackers store malicious SQL statements in a guest user’s graph display preferences.
  • These preferences are processed by Cacti, executing the SQL.
  • The SQL modifies the poller configuration to run arbitrary OS commands.
  • “I found a path from a fresh, unauthenticated HTTP session to command execution as the Cacti server user in four requests. No login. No valid API key. No phishing. Just four HTTP requests against the default guest surface,” explains the researcher.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Exploit name: 4HTTP2SHELL (previously 4HTTP2ROOT).
  • Published on Thanksgiving Day by researcher ek0ms savi0r from the Church of Malware.
  • GitHub repository: Sad Girls 0day Club.
  • Tested against Cacti Core 1.2.31; earlier versions may also be vulnerable.
  • The researcher expressed frustration: “Security researchers are not the bad guys. We’re the ones trying to help. We’re the ones who read the docs, wrote the repro, and sent the packet capture,” and “We get cracked because we get gaslit for years by billion dollar companies that treat disclosure like a PR problem.”

🚀 Availability

  • Public PoC released with a video demonstration.
  • The vulnerability was not reported to Cacti before its public release.

💡 Why it Matters

  • Cacti can store credentials and SNMP passphrases used to access network devices; a compromise could expose other systems.
  • Privileges gained depend on the account running the Cacti web server and poller processes; often a low‑privileged web server account rather than root.

📌 Mitigation

  • Deactivate the Cacti guest account.
  • Restrict access to the application’s web interface to trusted networks.
  • Review poller configurations for unexpected commands.
  • Examine application logs for warnings involving non‑numeric values in graph display settings, which could indicate attempted exploitation.

As of November 27, there have been no reports of the vulnerability being exploited in attacks.

#ZeroDay #Cacti #SQLInjection #Cybersecurity #NetworkMonitoring

Source: Unpatched Cacti zero-day with public PoC gives remote code execution

item.title: 12-Year-Old Linux NFS Vulnerability Lets Remote Attackers Gain Root
item.description:
12-Year-Old Linux NFS Vulnerability Lets Remote Attackers Gain Root

A 12‑year‑old critical vulnerability in the Linux kernel’s NFS server, CVE‑2026‑99362, lets remote attackers gain root privileges.

🔍 Overview

  • The flaw, dubbed NFS2ROOT by OpenSec, is a heap buffer overflow in the nfsd server.
  • Remote attackers can send crafted requests that write beyond an allocated buffer.
  • Successful exploitation corrupts kernel memory and grants root access on exposed Linux servers.

🧩 How it Works

  • An attacker sends malicious NFSv4.1 requests causing the server to write past a buffer.
  • This allows reading of kernel memory, bypassing KASLR.
  • A callback is placed in a released memory area that executes a command.
  • When the connection closes, the kernel runs the embedded command with root privileges.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Vulnerability exists since Linux kernel 3.16 (March 2014).
  • Affects kernels older than 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2, or 7.4‑rc1 when nfsd (v4.1 or 4.2) is loaded and TCP port 2049 is reachable over the Internet.
  • No user interaction required; low‑complexity attack.

🚀 Availability

  • ANSSI’s Jérémy Jean submitted a fix in August; the patch was shared with NFSD maintainers in late September.

💡 Why it Matters

  • No wild exploitation reports yet, but the flaw can give attackers full control.
  • Apply the latest kernel security updates immediately and reboot.
  • If patching isn’t possible, restrict TCP port 2049 to trusted clients or disable nfs-server in /etc/nfs.conf.
  • Kernel hardening does not remove the overflow; patch every host.
  • Monitor for signs such as kernel warnings from nfsd4_check_resp_size, shells spawned by kernel workers, bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions, and kernel oopses with nfsd4_* or svc_* frames.

📚 Related Flaws

  • Other privilege escalation bugs disclosed this year include RefluXFS, CIFSwitch, Dirty Frag, Fragnesia, PinTheft, Copy Fail, Pack2TheRoot, and DirtyDecrypt/DirtyCBC.

#Linux #NFS #KernelSecurity #CVE202699362 #PrivilegeEscalation #CyberSecurity

Source: New NFS2ROOT Linux flaw can let attackers gain root privileges

item.title: Major US Infrastructure Outages Are Coincidence, Not Cyberattack
item.description:
Major US Infrastructure Outages Are Coincidence, Not Cyberattack

A recent series of outages affecting major US infrastructure providers, including Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, an unnamed NSA network, and Apple, has raised suspicions of a coordinated cyberattack or conspiracy. Evidence indicates these incidents are unrelated and not the result of any cyberattack, nor are they caused by AI. The failures are attributed to a series of unfortunate coincidences involving old, incrementally patched systems often maintained by hobbyists without adequate backup systems.

🔍 Overview

It has been a difficult week for computerized infrastructure, with outages spanning critical sectors such as aviation, banking, and government. While the simultaneity of these events might suggest a common cause or conspiracy, the evidence clarifies that the incidents are distinct and unrelated. Notably, the failures are not the result of any cyberattack, coordinated or otherwise, and even more surprisingly, they do not seem to be the result of AI.

⚙️ Key Details

The underlying causes of these failures stem from the nature of the technology itself:

  • Age and Maintenance: Much of the infrastructure is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over decades.
  • Volunteer Maintenance: A surprising amount of the system is maintained by hobbyists without any recompense.
  • Lack of Redundancy: There often aren’t good backup systems.
  • Centralization: More of the infrastructure is centralized, meaning individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of life and society.
  • Brittleness: Much of the tech infrastructure just barely works; when it fails, it can fail badly.

💡 Why It Matters

Security, safety, resilience, redundancy, and recoverability are essential parts of reliable technology, but they are costs that do not generate near-term profits. Modern shareholder capitalism, particularly private equity, prioritizes near-term profits, squeezing out apparent inefficiencies and positive intangibles. Market competition, which usually nudges companies to provide better services, is often removed in pursuit of these profits. From a quarterly budget perspective, spending on reliability measures is viewed as an inefficiency or waste. Consequently, costs of failure are often pushed onto society, leading to stranded travelers and inaccessible bank accounts. These economic pressures create brittle systems with single points of failure, making them more susceptible to cyberattacks and random mistakes. Fixing these issues requires regulation with enforcement and meaningful fines, as well as stringent antitrust enforcement.

Entity Status

FAA Experienced outage
A handful of banks Experienced outage
United Airlines Experienced outage
Unnamed classified NSA network Experienced outage; details likely never public
Apple Experienced outage

item.title: SAP Confirms Cyberattack Involving Source Code Modification
item.description:
SAP Confirms Cyberattack Involving Source Code Modification

SAP has confirmed taking urgent action to protect its customers after detecting suspicious activity in its IT environment, a cyberattack the company tracks under the code name “Project Granite.”

🏢 Company Profile

SAP is one of the world’s largest enterprise software vendors, based in Walddorf, Germany. Key operational details include:

  • Employees: 110,000 across 157 countries
  • Subscribers: 300 million
  • Annual Revenue: Over $40 billion

🔍 Incident Details

According to reports from Der Spiegel, which accessed an internal SAP memo, the attackers breached SAP’s GitHub environment, potentially with the aid of AI tools. Insider sources indicated that authentications tokens were stolen from SAP employees and used to copy and modify source code on GitHub.

Aspect Detail
Internal Code Name Project Granite
Breach Vector GitHub environment
Suspected Aid AI tools
Actions Taken by Attacker Stole authentication tokens; copied and modified source code

🛡️ Offical Response

SAP stated that it prompted all employees to keep project details confidential and implemented necessary measures to preserve service security. A company representative told BleepingComputer:

“SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services.”

Regarding the scope of the compromise, SAP noted:

“Based on our investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data.”

“Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on.”

Despite this, SAP has not specified which environments were observed having suspicious activity, nor has it advised customers downloading code or performing updates from specific repositories to take action. A spokesperson declined to share further information on this matter.

☣️ Context

The incident follows a public warning from Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) regarding agentic AI tools that empower cyberattacks, such as ARTEX, CAIRN, and PentAGI. This follows reports from Swiss and Italian national cybersecurity agencies regarding the first detections of large-scale AI-driven cyberattacks targeting critical infrastructure.

#SAP #Cybersecurity #DataBreach #AIsecurity

Source: SAP confirms security incident after suspicious GitHub activity

item.title: 1Password discloses breach after GitHub account compromise
item.description:
1Password discloses breach after GitHub account compromise

1Password disclosed a data breach after an employee’s corporate GitHub account was hacked. The attacker used the compromised account to deploy malicious code to the company’s backend services to steal customer data.

🔍 Overview

The company began investigating the breach on November 19 after detecting indications that an employee’s GitHub account had been compromised. 1Password states that customer password vaults and the encryption keys protecting them were not compromised in the attack.

🧩 How it works

The attacker accessed private source code repositories and injected malicious code into backend services that downloaded customer account records. The malicious code also stole internal company source code and accessed the company’s continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) environment, potentially exposing internal infrastructure credentials.

⚙️ Key details

The following customer data was stolen in the breach:

  • Customer names and email addresses
  • Account and user IDs
  • Account creation and last sign-in timestamps
  • Public cryptographic keys
  • Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol parameters
  • Invitation, provisioning, and account recovery tokens
  • Other internal account metadata

The stolen tokens were embedded in links that 1Password emailed to users to accept account provisioning invitations or recover their accounts. 1Password says these tokens cannot be used on their own to access customer accounts, as completing the invitation or recovery process requires either single sign-on (SSO) authentication or a six-digit verification code sent to the user’s registered email address.

🚀 Availability

1Password has disabled the compromised GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, restored clean versions of affected services, and rotated or revoked potentially exposed infrastructure credentials. The company has also hired independent cybersecurity experts to validate its remediation efforts. As a precaution against brute-force attacks, 1Password has strengthened these verification codes from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters. The company states that only a small number of users were affected and have been individually notified.

💡 Why it matters

While customer vaults were not compromised, the stolen data is valuable to threat actors as it provides a list of known 1Password users who could be targeted in phishing campaigns. Threat actors could send emails impersonating 1Password, using the breach as a lure to trick customers into disclosing their account passwords, Secret Keys, or recovery verification codes. 1Password is not requiring customers to change their account passwords or Secret Keys but warns them to watch for unexpected invitations, account recovery requests, and other potential phishing attempts.

#1Password #DataBreach #CyberSecurity #GitHub #Phishing

Source: 1Password customer data stolen after employee GitHub account breach

item.title: AI Agents Fuel Large-Scale Cyberattacks on European Critical Infrastructure
item.description:
AI Agents Fuel Large-Scale Cyberattacks on European Critical Infrastructure

Recent alerts from Swiss and Italian cybersecurity agencies confirm that autonomous AI agents are conducting large‑scale attacks on critical‑infrastructure organisations, using publicly available frameworks to find and exploit vulnerabilities quickly.

🔍 Overview

  • Swiss NCSC: first reports of AI‑assisted attacks on Swiss organisations, including critical infrastructure across at least two sectors.
  • “In recent days, the NCSC has received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland in which the attack was carried out with the assistance of an AI agent,” the Swiss NCSC said.
  • Various organisations and operators of critical infrastructure across at least two sectors have been affected by these cyberattacks.
  • In all cyberattacks known to the NCSC, the use of AI agents led to the successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems.
  • Italian CSIRT Italia: detected large‑scale campaigns using autonomous AI agents on exposed endpoints; observed multiple agents working in parallel; rapid attacks exploiting weak passwords and known vulnerabilities; AI chained vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, compromised credentials.
  • The agency described rapid attacks in which agents exploited weak passwords and known vulnerabilities in exposed endpoints, using frameworks to verify weaknesses and independently decide what to do next.
  • In some cases, the agency observed multiple AI agents working in parallel to compromise a large number of systems within a few hours.
  • In one instance involving a DeepSeek Harness setup, a coordinator assigned tasks to five AI agents that undertook a broad spectrum of operational stages, from information gathering to exploitation and persistence.
  • Agents chained vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and compromised credentials, leveraging exposed systems as a foothold to reach internal networks.

🧩 How it Works

“During the observed campaigns, autonomous agents demonstrated the ability to carry out complex, sustained activity to detect misconfigurations, link even low‑impact vulnerabilities into complex attack chains, and dynamically adapt their operating modules,” CSIRT Italia says.

“They went as far as writing malicious code in real time to evade endpoint defenses and carry out actions deeper within the infrastructure.”

⚙️ Key Details

Framework Involved in recent breaches and hacking incidents
ARTEX AI Yes
CyberStrikeAI Yes
DeepSeek Harness - Red Team Yes
PentAGI Yes
  • Reduce the number of systems exposed on the internet.
  • Prioritize patching, especially internet‑facing systems within 24 hours of release.
  • Add multi‑factor authentication (MFA) or passkey protection.
  • Enforce least‑privilege principles.
  • Disable remote management interfaces if not needed.
  • Monitor control‑plane operations, authentication sources, traffic to internal networks, and outbound server traffic.
  • The number of publicly available AI agents has nearly doubled since October, fueling large waves of attacks.

💡 Why it Matters

  • AI agents can rapidly identify and exploit vulnerabilities across many systems.
  • They chain low‑impact vulnerabilities into complex attack chains.
  • They can write malicious code in real time to evade defenses.
  • The attacks have already compromised IT systems in critical infrastructure.
  • Urgent mitigation is required to protect exposed assets.

#AIagents #Cybersecurity #CriticalInfrastructure #SwissNCSC #ItalianCSIRT

Source: Italy and Switzerland warn of autonomous AI-driven cyberattacks

item.title: Attackers Chain Exploits to Target Exposed Palo Alto Networks Devices
item.description:
Attackers Chain Exploits to Target Exposed Palo Alto Networks Devices

Threat actors are chaining exploits for the PHP2Shell and Fragnesia vulnerabilities to target Palo Alto Networks devices with management interfaces exposed to the internet.

🧩 How it works

The attacks combine two distinct security issues:

  • PHP2Shell: Two critical PHP vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. These allow unauthenticated attackers to run code remotely with the privileges of the PHP web worker.
  • Fragnesia: A Linux kernel vulnerability in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem (CVE-2026-46300) that lets a local attacker with low privileges escalate permissions to root level.

A November 28 alert from CISA warned that these issues were being chained to deploy PHP webshells on vulnerable systems and execute commands as root. Dream Security researchers reported observing a campaign using this specific chain, targeting servers in the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, including a U.S. government affiliate.

⚙️ Key details

  • Exploitation vector: Palo Alto Networks confirmed in an advisory that attacks target firewalls running PAN-OS with their management interface exposed to the public internet.
  • Exposure: The company stated that all observed exploitation activity involved devices that exposed their management interface to the public internet, contrary to recommended best practices.
  • Chaining specifics: While technical details of the chaining were not provided, Palo Alto Networks noted that the observed method is the only known way to exploit the Fragnesia flaw.

🛡️ Mitigation

  • PHP2Shell update: Administrators who already applied updates addressing the PHP2Shell flaw are considered safe from these specific chained attacks.
  • Fragnesia fixes: Fixes have been released for PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1, and 12.2, with the exact patch-carrying build varying by release.
  • Network configuration: For those requiring a remote management interface, Palo Alto Networks recommends restricting access to trusted internal IP addresses.

#Cybersecurity #PaloAltoNetworks #CVE #ZeroDay #SecurityVulnerability

Source: Palo Alto Networks warns of Fragnesia flaw exploited in PAN-OS attacks

item.title: AI-Driven Cyberattacks Shift from Theory to Real-World Execution
item.description:
AI-Driven Cyberattacks Shift from Theory to Real-World Execution

AI-driven attacks are on the rise, transitioning from theoretical risks to real-world threats. Recent investigations reveal that criminals are using AI to accelerate attacks at scale, with attackers leveraging AI agents to execute context-aware commands with real-time decision-making.

🔍 Overview

In one observed campaign, a highly persistent threat actor utilized AI to generate 117 unique scripts across multiple languages and executed over 8,000 unique commands in just 12 days. This volume significantly exceeds the capabilities of normal attackers, who usually execute dozens of commands with a few scripts over similar periods.

⚙️ Key Details

The observed attack campaign featured two distinct phases, characterized by different execution styles:

Phase Characteristics Execution Metrics
Human Attacker Made typographical errors, repeated manual checks, demonstrated environment confusion Median time between commands roughly 24 seconds
Agentic Phase Flawless, zero-syntax-error commands Median gap between commands just 1.4 seconds

When instructed to execute aspects of an attack, the AI agent rapidly scans networks, attempts to elevate privileges, and utilizes legitimate native tools to blend in.

💡 Why It Matters

Attack isolation and near real-time response are now critical mandates. If defenders wait hours to react, an AI agent can already have enumerated cloud infrastructure and extracted or encrypted data. To effectively defend against these threats, defenders must employ AI-powered tools.

Leveraging AI on the edge—specifically on endpoints and Next-Generation Firewalls (NGFW)—is a major strategic necessity. Edge-based AI can process telemetry instantly, making split-second decisions to terminate malicious web shell sessions or block active privilege escalation attempts locally. In observed product deployments, edge AI operated in milliseconds rather than the minutes required by agentic LLMs.

Furthermore, local edge AI maintains detection coverage even if an attack vector is used to temporarily disable network traffic to operate silently. This approach enables defenders to catch and isolate threats at the earliest possible stage and safeguards sensitive corporate data locally without requiring telemetry or proprietary data to be transmitted to the cloud for analysis.

🧩 Defense Strategy

Despite their speed, agentic AI attackers have a foundational weakness: they enter the environment without information. Defenders hold an upper hand through comprehensive AI analytics.

  • Data Normalization: Collecting telemetry across diverse network, endpoint, identity, and cloud sources to map distinct data streams into a single, cohesive schema.
  • Advanced Stitching: Merging related events across disparate sensors into unified, context-rich stories rather than disconnected events.
  • Baseline Establishment: AI analytics engines make it easier to create and update baselines.
  • Automated Response: Organizations must combine real-time detection with automated response capabilities, enabling instant attack isolation and automated remediation before critical systems or data are compromised.

#Cybersecurity #AIAgents #EdgeAI #ThreatDetection #NetworkSecurity

Source: The AI Threat Horizon: Why Speed, Edge AI and Baselines Are Our Best Defense

item.title: CIA and FinCEN Report Cyberattacks Using ARTEX Framework
item.description:
CIA and FinCEN Report Cyberattacks Using ARTEX Framework

Unknown attackers breached an open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis system at the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and also affected the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency. Additionally, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed an investigation into unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.

🔍 Overview

  • The cyberattack was reportedly carried out using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing framework.
  • The incident affected the CIA, the ODNI, and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.
  • FinCEN is a US Department of the Treasury bureau that acts as the country’s official Financial Intelligence Unit and protects the nation’s financial system from illicit activities.

⚙️ Key details

  • The CIA and ODNI have not yet replied to a request for more details regarding the incident.
  • No classified data or systems were exposed in the breach.
  • A source stated, “The hack did not involve our classified networks or classified information, and no other systems are currently at risk.”

item.title: Eclypsium Report: Most Infrastructure Security Fixes Address Bundled Software Flaws
item.description:
Eclypsium Report: Most Infrastructure Security Fixes Address Bundled Software Flaws

Eclypsium’s November InfraTrust Pulse report indicates that the majority of infrastructure security advisories addressing exploited vulnerabilities over the past month involve flaws in third-party software bundled into products rather than code developed by the vendors themselves.

🔍 Overview

The report tracks 373 new security advisories published by 23 infrastructure vendors between October 15 and November 19, covering 3,880 vulnerabilities. Of these advisories, 98 were rated critical, and 38 contained vulnerabilities listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. However, 33 of those 38 advisories fixed exploited flaws in bundled software components, primarily PHP, Node.js, and OpenSSH.

⚙️ Key Details

These vulnerabilities pose additional risks for enterprises because, even after a software developer releases a security fix, organizations must wait for infrastructure vendors to incorporate it into their products. “Your exposure to exploited flaws depends on how quickly each vendor rebuilds its products after an upstream fix ships,” the report reads. As of November 20, PHP2Shell fixes were either partially available or had yet to be released for affected products from Fortinet, Juniper, Lenovo, HPE, Netgear, HP, and Siemens. The November 19 release of another 18 PHP security advisories further complicated patching efforts for infrastructure vendors and their customers.

🚨 Active Exploitations

Threat actors are chaining PHP vulnerabilities with other flaws to gain root access to compromised devices. An example is the two PHP vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) highlighted in last month’s InfraTrust report, which are now being exploited in attacks against Palo Alto Networks and Check Point firewalls. Check Point reported that destructive attacks deployed data-wiping malware on VMware ESXi hosts. Other notable active exploits include:

  • Cisco Expressway: CVE-2026-76466, a critical vulnerability added to CISA’s KEV catalog on November 20. On November 23, CISA flagged this flaw as actively exploited after Russian cybersecurity firm F6 spotted hackers using it to gain root privileges.
  • Palo Alto Networks and Check Point: The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and CVE-2026-123039 in Check Point gateways. Check Point warned that this flaw was being actively exploited to gain root privileges and establish persistence on vulnerable devices since late October.
  • Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator: CVE-2026-114625, a critical vulnerability with a CVSS score of 9.9 that was exploited in zero-day attacks.
  • Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and FTD: CVE-2026-76418, affecting devices configured for remote-access VPNs. The flaw was exploited in attacks to crash devices.
  • SonicWall SonicOS: CVE-2026-19868, allowing multifactor authentication bypass on VPNs configured with single sign-on. SonicWall warned that it received reports that the flaw was exploited in zero-day attacks.

💡 Recommendations

Administrators should also prioritize installing Fortinet’s October hardening updates, which addressed numerous vulnerabilities discovered using AI models. As AI makes it easier to discover and exploit vulnerabilities, InfraTrust warns that organizations must take additional steps to protect their devices while waiting for vendors to release security updates. These include:

  • Removing management interfaces from the Internet
  • Segmenting them internally to limit lateral movement
  • Investigating previously exposed devices for backdoors that may remain even after security updates are installed

“Patching is table stakes, but what you do before the patch is available and after the exploit hits will determine whether you survive,” the report concludes.

item.title: Attackers Weaponize Autonomous AI Agents in 10 Global Campaigns
item.description:
Attackers Weaponize Autonomous AI Agents in 10 Global Campaigns

Attackers are weaponizing autonomous AI agents in real-world campaigns, creating a risk that until recently has only been theoretical. Between July and September 2026, more than 10 global campaigns were identified and tracked in which different attackers deployed autonomous AI agents to enhance their attacks.

🔍 Overview

These agentic AI attackers operated at machine speed, compressing the attack lifecycle from weeks or days into mere hours. The campaigns targeted diverse sectors, including government, logistics, hospitality, manufacturing, agriculture, and education.

In every observed campaign, attackers gained their initial foothold through web shells that were deployed via vulnerable web applications. The novelty of these agentic campaigns was not in their techniques, but in their speed and efficiency. The AI-driven operators matched the tradecraft of proficient human attackers while operating at machine scale, at times executing hundreds of unique commands in just minutes.

🧩 How It Works

An agentic AI attacker is an autonomous AI system—usually a large language model (LLM) with tool-calling capabilities—that independently plans, executes, and adapts attack sequences without continuous human guidance. Unlike chatbots that respond to individual prompts, agentic AI systems operate in a loop: they observe their environment, reason about what to do next, take action, and then observe the results to inform their next step.

The typical operational flow includes:

  • Human sets the objective: The human operator identifies a target and provides initial access, typically a web shell on a vulnerable web application.
  • AI agent takes over: The AI agent autonomously performs further reconnaissance, credential harvesting, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.
  • AI agent reports back: The AI agent structures its findings using machine-readable output formatting and periodically checks in with orchestration APIs.
  • Human makes strategic decisions: The human operator reviews the AI agent’s findings and directs high-level strategy, such as instructing the agent to target the payment system or establish persistence.
  • AI agent executes: The AI agent carries out the human’s strategic directives with tactical autonomy.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Speed and scale: An agentic AI attacker operates at machine speed. In the observed campaigns, AI agents executed hundreds of unique commands within minutes.
  • Lowered barrier to entry: Attackers can provide high-level guidance while the AI agent automates intricate technical phases, including compiling kernel exploits, navigating cross-platform lateral movement, and systematically compromising cloud infrastructure.
  • Adaptive reasoning: Unlike script-based attacks that fail when they encounter unexpected conditions, agentic AI attackers employ reasoning to try alternative approaches when failures occur. Agents were observed attempting five different privilege escalation techniques in sequence when earlier ones failed, and compiling custom exploit code on-target when pre-built binaries didn’t work.
  • Cross-domain fluency: A single agentic AI attacker can operate across Linux, Windows, various cloud platforms, web applications, databases, and network infrastructures.
  • Behavioral fingerprints: Using AI agents came at the expense of operational stealth. The agents left unmistakable behavioral fingerprints that revealed the involvement of non-human operators, including:
    • Structured machine-readable output formats.
    • Adaptive exploit selection.
    • Iterative refinement.
    • Chain-of-thought reasoning comments that appeared in shell commands.

💡 Why It Matters

New challenges in threat attribution have emerged because AI agents generate unique, dynamic payloads on the fly without distinct behavioral fingerprints, making it increasingly difficult to attribute attacks to specific threat actors.

item.title: Law enforcement disrupts 57 illegal IPTV services across 11 countries
item.description:
Law enforcement disrupts 57 illegal IPTV services across 11 countries

Law enforcement authorities from 11 countries have disrupted 57 illegal streaming services that operated hundreds of websites and drew over 7.3 million visits each year. The joint operation targeted a criminal market where unauthorized access to premium television channels, live sports, and films is sold via illegal IPTV services, often using cryptocurrency for subscription payments.

📋 Operation details

According to a Tuesday press release from Europol, the operation resulted in the following:

  • 57 illegal IPTV services were disrupted.
  • 321 websites illegally offering copyrighted content were identified.
  • Combined annual traffic of the targeted sites exceeded 7.3 million visits.
  • Investigators traced over €26 million in cryptocurrency transactions, with further analysis ongoing.

The investigation involved tracing links between illegal IPTV services, crypto wallets, financial transactions, and the individuals controlling the services. These operators used wallets to receive and transfer payments to move money between countries and obscure the origin of their profits.

🤝 Partners involved

The operation was a joint action involving Europol, the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO), INTERPOL, and the European Audiovisual Anti-Piracy Alliance (AAPA). To trace cryptocurrency payments and identify financial networks, investigators partnered with crypto industry experts from Binance, Coinbase, and Chainalysis.

📉 Impact on legitimate providers

According to the AAPA, legitimate service providers lose around €4.83 billion annually as roughly 60 million people in Europe use illegal platforms for streaming content. These illegal services typically charge a small monthly fee for access to content that has not been licensed by copyright owners.

item.title: Microsoft: Azure API Management vulnerability used to steal credentials
item.description:
Microsoft: Azure API Management vulnerability used to steal credentials

Microsoft has issued a security advisory warning that a vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) Classic tiers was exploited to steal stored API credentials, with Norwegian authorities linking the flaw to cyberattacks against energy companies. The issue affects a cloud service that allows organizations to publish, secure, monitor, and manage APIs connecting applications, services, and data.

🔍 Overview

In a security advisory with Tracking ID MZK9-GH0, Microsoft stated it identified the vulnerability on November 18, 2026, and deployed a mitigation the following day. The company confirmed that customers were exposed and that an unauthorized party could have accessed secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before the issue was identified.

⚙️ Key details

  • Affected Tiers: The vulnerability specifically affects Azure API Management Classic tiers; Microsoft stated that APIM v2 tiers are not impacted.
  • Access Mechanism: The flaw allowed unauthorized access to certain management functionality when APIM Classic instances were not configured according to recommended security best practices.
  • Potential Impact: This access could allow attackers to perform administrative operations, including accessing secrets, which could potentially grant access to additional applications, services, or backend systems depending on permissions.
  • Remediation: Microsoft closed the unauthorized access path on November 19 and rotated Microsoft-controlled keys and credentials where appropriate.
  • Limitation: The remediation does not automatically invalidate customer credentials that may have been accessed before the fix was deployed.

🏛️ Reported Exploitation

Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) linked the vulnerability to attacks affecting Norwegian organizations, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi.

  • NSM Advisory: The agency stated that an unknown threat actor targeted access tokens, secrets, and named values stored in Azure API Management.
  • Discovery: NSM reported that Norway’s energy sector first discovered the vulnerability, noting that organizations in other countries and industries were also affected.
  • Equinor: The company disclosed an ongoing cyberattack on November 17, the day before Microsoft identified the vulnerability. Equinor later announced it had stopped the attack and found no indication that data had been stolen or altered.
  • Skagerak Energi: The company reported an attempted cyberattack but stated it had no impact on operations and no evidence that information was compromised.

Additionally, a Reddit post from an administrator alleged their organization detected unauthorized access to Azure Key Vault using a valid administrator token. The administrator claimed attackers exploited a zero-day authentication bypass in a deprecated legacy API to gain access to a privileged system account on APIM instances. They alleged the legacy API did not generate logs for customers to detect this access and that Microsoft initially attributed the activity to leaked customer credentials. BleepingComputer has not independently verified these allegations.

💡 Recommendations

Microsoft urged affected customers to:

  • Immediately rotate potentially exposed credentials.
  • Investigate suspicious activity in systems accessible through those credentials.
  • Review available logs for signs of unauthorized access.

NSM warned organizations to verify that their APIM instances have received the security update, noting that instances running below specific runtime versions remain vulnerable. The agency advised customers to contact their service provider if they have not received the update. Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen has shared threat-hunting queries to help organizations investigate potential exploitation and identify stored credentials.

item.title: Recent cyber incidents not linked to AI
item.description:
Recent cyber incidents not linked to AI

Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, the NSA—it’s been a really bad week in cyberspace.

🔍 Overview

  • But, amazing as it might seem, these are not related.
  • As far as we know, they’re not the result of cyberattacks.
  • They’re not even related to AI.

⚙️ Infrastructure Challenges

  • Our computerized infrastructure is vulnerable and fragile.
  • Much of it is old, and has been incrementally patched and upgraded.
  • A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense.
  • And more and more of it is centralized: the same systems affecting many different aspects of our lives and society.
  • In many cases, it just barely works.
  • And when it fails, it tends to fail badly.

💡 Economic Drivers

  • There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream of the economic ones.
  • The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problem lies.
  • Security, safety, resilience, redundancy, recoverability—these are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs.
  • More importantly, they are inefficient: costs that feel wasteful until something bad happens.
  • Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, squeeze all inefficiencies out of a company in pursuit of near‑term profits.
  • Competition, with multiple companies competing to do the same thing, is another inefficiency.
  • Monopolization removes that in pursuit of near‑term profits.

🔧 Risks and Failures

  • The result is brittle systems, single points of failure.
  • They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI‑fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes.
  • The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.

🔄 The Path Forward

  • Fixing this is technical, but it’s political first.
  • It requires changing incentives, and that involves regulation and control.

#Cybersecurity #AI #Infrastructure #Capitalism #Regulation

item.title: Threat actors compromised 24 Check Point servers across 22 organizations in cyberespionage campaign
item.description:
Threat actors compromised 24 Check Point servers across 22 organizations in cyberespionage campaign

Threat actors exploited multiple vulnerabilities to compromise two dozen Check Point Security management servers in an ongoing campaign targeting 22 organizations, according to threat intelligence firm GreyNoise. The activity, tracked as GT13, was confirmed as ongoing between October 17 and November 2, though researchers believe the campaign remains active given the threat actors’ persistent access to Check Point devices. The 22 victim organizations are spread across 17 countries and include government entities, financial services providers, and companies in the energy, transportation, mining, and manufacturing sectors.

🔍 Overview

The attackers launched their operations from 99 IP addresses that appear to come from compromised Check Point devices and ExpressVPN exit nodes. GreyNoise detected the activity and noted it resembled cyberespionage operations, although the attacker’s motivation could not be conclusively determined. The researchers assessed that GT13 operated an AI-powered offensive tool, based on observed behavior, automation, and custom tooling, but this use of AI in the campaign remains unconfirmed.

🧩 How it works

The attack chain began with unknown means of initial compromise, though GreyNoise could not determine when or how the Check Point servers were breached. During post-compromise stages, the researchers observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-16232, an authentication bypass in Check Point SmartConsole that allows attackers to obtain an application login token and authenticate with administrator privileges. A Rejetto HTTP File Server, compromised by exploiting CVE-2026-61500, was used as an operational relay for managing intrusions and collecting stolen data from the compromised environments.

⚙️ Key details

The attackers leveraged automation and custom tooling, observed across more than 1,400 network sessions, 800 command-line artifacts, and 1,200 file-related activities. Their activities included:

  • Stealing firewall databases, credentials, configuration data, and internal certificate authority files
  • Generating a new certificate in one victim’s environment
  • Unloading security policies, effectively disabling firewall protections
  • Conducting internal network reconnaissance and attempting lateral movement

On October 26, the attacker performed a bulk certificate management operation across all 24 compromised Check Point servers, which failed, but still helped GreyNoise identify victims. The researchers also observed attempts to exploit multiple additional vulnerabilities: CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF), and CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script).

The campaign targeted additional enterprise systems including:

System Vulnerability Notes
Citrix NetScaler CVE-2023-4966 Targeted in lateral movement
Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2024-21893 Targeted during campaign
VMware vCenter CVE-2021-21972, CVE-2023-34048 Multiple vulnerabilities exploited
Microsoft Exchange CVE-2021-26855/34473 Targeted during intrusions
Microsoft Netlogon CVE-2020-1472 Part of lateral movement attempts

BleepingComputer has contacted Check Point to ask if they have better visibility into those attacks and which flaw was exploited for initial access, and we are waiting for their response.

💡 Why it matters

Although GreyNoise lost visibility into the campaign operations on November 2, the researchers believe it could still be ongoing. The company has notified international government partners and CERTs to alert impacted organizations and shared indicators of compromise (IoCs) that could help identify additional intrusions or block future attempts. Check Point warned about CVE-2026-16232 in July, marking it as an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability.

The campaign demonstrates sophisticated attack capabilities using compromised infrastructure and automation tools to conduct large-scale credential theft and lateral movement across critical infrastructure sectors including government, finance, and energy.

item.title: Authorities Warn More Major Tech Outages Likely as AI-Driven Upgrades Create System Vulnerability
item.description:
Authorities Warn More Major Tech Outages Likely as AI-Driven Upgrades Create System Vulnerability

Recent weeks have seen a cascade of high-profile disruptions—including a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage, and a JPMorgan Chase banking outage—prompting US intelligence and tech leaders to warn that more such events are inevitable.

📢 Official Warnings

item.description:
CrowdSec provides open-source IDS/IPS and WAF with community blocklists

CrowdSec is an open-source, participative security solution that offers crowdsourced server detection and protection against malicious IPs. It operates as an all-in-one IDS/IPS and WAF for Linux, Windows, Docker, and Kubernetes environments, allowing users to detect bad behaviors and actively remediate threats through a shared community blocklist.

🔍 Overview

  • CrowdSec is an open-source security solution that is participative by design.
  • It provides IDS/IPS (Intrusion Detection/Prevention System) and WAF (Web Application Firewall) capabilities.
  • It supports Linux, Windows, Docker, and Kubernetes.
  • It features a crowdsourced blocklist of malicious IPs.
  • Detection rules are available under the MIT license.

🧩 How it works

  • Log Analysis: The Security Engine detects bad behaviors by analyzing log sources and HTTP requests.
  • Decoupled Architecture: Following a “Detect Here, Remedy There” approach, users can parse logs on one machine and block threats at a firewall, reverse proxy, or CDN on another.
  • WAF Capabilities: The AppSec component is built on Coraza, allowing SecLang rules and the OWASP Core Rule Set to load as-is. It also supports a YAML rule format.
  • Bot Mitigation: AppSec can answer suspicious requests with a JavaScript proof-of-work challenge at tunable difficulty, stopping headless browsers and scrapers while allowing verified crawlers like Googlebot to pass.
  • Community Blocklist: An IP identified as malicious by one user is added to a curated list, proactively blocking that IP for all other users before it reaches their systems.

⚙️ Key details

  • Scenarios: Ships by default with scenarios for brute force, port scan, and web scan.
  • Customization: Users can extend protection by picking more scenarios from the Hub or creating their own.
  • Remediation: Allows active remediation using Remediation Components.
  • Comparison: Unlike fail2ban, CrowdSec decouples detection and remediation; unlike ModSecurity or naxsi, it shares IP reputation and remediation layers with the log-based engine.

🚀 Availability

  • Installation is available for Linux, Windows, Docker, OpnSense, and Kubernetes.
  • The Community Blocklist is available in real-time.
  • Detection rules are hosted on the CrowdSec Hub.

Microsoft Suffers Data Breach Following Entra Connect Health Vulnerability

Microsoft is warning organizations that it suffered a data breach after attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Entra Connect Health service to gain unauthorized access to administrator email addresses and tenant configuration information.

🔍 Overview

  • Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a cloud-based monitoring service that allows administrators to monitor the health, performance, and alerts of their on-premises identity infrastructure through the Microsoft Entra admin center.

  • Microsoft concluded its investigation on November 20, 2026, determining that unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata occurred, with no unauthorized configuration changes identified.

  • Tenant IDs, display names, initial domain names, country codes, and regional information were exposed.

  • Connect Health onboarding status was exposed.
  • An expired certificate previously used to register Connect Health agents with a Microsoft internal service that was decommissioned in late 2024 was exposed.
  • User passwords, password hashes, authentication tokens, valid cryptographic keys, on-premises server and Active Directory topology details, and Azure subscription information were not exposed.

🛠️ Timeline and Remediation

  • Microsoft deployed a server-side fix on November 19, 2026, to prevent further exploitation.
  • Microsoft finished its investigation on November 20 and began notifying affected organizations.
  • No software updates or other customer remediation are required to address the vulnerability.
  • Microsoft published a PowerShell script at https://aka.ms/ConnectHealth/scripts allowing administrators to view the types of tenant metadata that could have been exposed.

💡 Recommendations

  • Alert security teams to potential targeted phishing and social-engineering attacks targeting exposed administrator email addresses and tenant information.

item.title: OpenNHP toolkit hides infrastructure using zero-trust cryptography
item.description:
OpenNHP toolkit hides infrastructure using zero-trust cryptography

OpenNHP is a lightweight, cryptography-powered, open-source toolkit implementing Zero Trust security for infrastructure, applications, and data. It serves as the reference implementation of the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) Network-infrastructure Hiding Protocol (NHP) specification.

🔍 Overview

OpenNHP is designed to hide servers, ports, and domains from the public internet. In the AI era, visibility equates to vulnerability; OpenNHP inverts this model by remaining invisible until trusted. Consequently, scanners, bots, and AI-driven attackers find nothing to attack because nothing answers until a client proves its identity with a single encrypted packet.

🧩 How it works

The toolkit features two core protocols and a modular design inspired by the NIST Zero Trust Architecture:

  • Network-infrastructure Hiding Protocol (NHP): Conceals server ports, IP addresses, and domain names to protect applications and infrastructure from unauthorized access.
  • Data-content Hiding Protocol (DHP): Ensures data security and privacy via encryption and confidential computing, making data “usable but not visible.”

The architecture includes specific components that slot alongside existing IAM, DNS, FIDO, and Zero Trust policy engines:

Component Function
NHP-Agent Client that sends encrypted knock requests to gain access
NHP-Server Authenticates and authorizes requests; runs separately and is architecturally decoupled from the protected host
NHP-AC Access controller that manages firewall rules on the protected server
NHP-Relay HTTP-to-UDP bridge enabling browser-based agents to send NHP knocks via HTTPS
NHP-KGC Key Generation Center for Identity-Based Cryptography (IBC)

The workflow operates on a default-deny gate for every port, IP, and hostname:

  1. Registration (once per device): The agent generates its own key pair and enrolls the public key. The agent requests a one-time password (NHP_OTP), which the Server’s auth plugin delivers to the user (e.g., by email). The agent sends the OTP and its public key (NHP_REG), and the Server binds the key to the user and replies (NHP_RAK). The private key never leaves the device.
  2. Knock (every access): The agent sends an encrypted knock (NHP_KNK) to the Server. The Server validates the knock and sends an operation.

💡 Why it matters

Attackers can’t exploit what they can’t discover. NHP represents a next step in “hide the service first” designs, extending security stacks rather than forking them.

item.title: AI Formal Verification Tools Combat Code Slop and Security Risks
item.description:
AI Formal Verification Tools Combat Code Slop and Security Risks

The term “slop” has become the industry’s word of the year for 2026, describing low-quality output from large language models. As AI-generated code increases, software engineers are turning to formal verification systems—tools that use mathematical proofs and logic to ensure correctness—to mitigate this daily concern.

🧩 How it works

Formal verification relies on “solvers” for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT). The most prominent is cvc5, an automated reasoning engine co-created by Stanford Corbel Professor (Research) of Computer Science Clark Barrett.

  • cvc5 is widely used in companies like Amazon, including in specification analysis and test generation for Kiro, Amazon’s agentic development environment.
  • A new entrant, &Truth (pronounced ‘and truth’), builds on Lean, an open-source programming language and proof assistant. &Truth combines AI with automated reasoning to construct proofs that Lean checks, aiming to create a “verification machine” that reads code in any language to prove it satisfies stated requirements.
  • Axiom Math develops AxiomProver, an AI system that generates Lean proofs, alongside AXLE, a toolkit for manipulating those proofs. Axiom uses formal verification to provide correctness feedback for training its mathematical reasoning systems.
  • Harmonic’s automated theorem prover, Aristotle, uses Lean heavily, ensuring that AI writes proofs while Lean checks every step, so results never rest on the AI being right.

⚙️ Key details

  • Theorem focuses on cybersecurity, stating that “Verification is the only defense that holds while adversaries scale.” It has collaborated with Anthropic on formal software verification at scale.
  • &Truth prioritizes cybersecurity, including scanning C code to ensure memory safety.
  • Lean is increasingly used by frontier models to solve difficult math problems. For instance, GPT-6.2 Astra produced what is believed to be the first Lean proof of Smoktunowicz’s Gap Theorem, and Anthropic used Lean to formalize Fermat’s Last Theorem in a 13-million-line project.
  • Anthropic reported that Opus 5.5 achieved a 50% solve rate on 36 small verification tasks using about 40% fewer tokens than Opus 5, with a collaboration with Theorem describing “LLM-scaled formal verification” as a promising approach for security guarantees.

#FormalVerification #AI #Lean #Cybersecurity #cvc5

item.title: Amazon Threat Intelligence details AI agent hack on universities
item.description:
Amazon Threat Intelligence details AI agent hack on universities

Amazon Threat Intelligence shared findings from an investigation into a Chinese-nexus threat actor who used autonomous AI agents to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The investigation revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over a 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026.

🔍 Overview

On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet. This visibility included project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time.

🧩 How it works

Cairn is built as a research and problem-solving engine for defenders. Operating it is simple: given a starting point and an objective in plain language, it coordinates multiple AI agents to find a path to that goal. The actor in this campaign gave the agents a simple goal: “obtain shell access.” Based on a list of targeted IP addresses and that goal, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step.

⚙️ Key details

The campaign included several operations that varied widely in complexity and outcome. During the campaign, the agents found a zero-day in an open-source application and used it to gain full control of a server.

Operation Target Duration Key Actions
Redis instance at one university ~16 hours 148 sequential actions; abused replication feature, escaped scripting sandbox, wrote to config files, corrupted memory, attempted Log4Shell injection
University GPU server > 6 hours Researched public presence to build list of ~80 usernames; tested > 30,000 credential combinations against SSH, admin dashboard, network storage, VPN, and campus portal
Open-source medical imaging AI application Not specified Identified framework, mapped API endpoints, found upload endpoint with a filename parameter

In the Redis operation, when initial attempts to take control failed, the agents mapped the internal Docker network topology through a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance and launched credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and several other services. None of these attempts succeeded. In the GPU server operation, the agents never found a working login. Against the medical imaging application, the agents successfully identified the framework and mapped its API endpoints.

💡 Why it matters

These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening. Defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable, as the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction, even when specific operations did not succeed.

#Cybersecurity #AIAgents #ThreatIntelligence #Amazon #Zero-day #AutonomousHacking

BADBOX 3.0 Botnet Returns with Record Ad Fraud Activity

The BADBOX malware botnet has resurfaced, generating a record 40 billion fraudulent advertising bid requests per day through infected Android-based devices.

🔍 Overview

  • The BADBOX 3.0 variant has grown into the largest documented ad-fraud operation by daily bid request volume.
  • It was first discovered in early 2023 on a T95 Android TV box bought on Amazon.
  • Germany’s cybersecurity agencies warned in December 2024 that the botnet had infected tens of thousands of devices.

  • Google later sued the botnet’s operators, saying the BADBOX 2.0 had infected over 10 million Android-based devices by April 2025.

🧩 How it works

  • The malware performs ad fraud by playing video ads in hidden windows while impersonating legitimate streaming apps to make the requests appear legitimate.
  • HUMAN also observed fraudulent server-side ad insertion (SSAI) requests that tricked advertisers into believing ads were played on streaming devices, even though no actual device or video ad was involved.
  • A proxying module also enrolled infected devices in one of 11 residential proxy networks without the owners’ knowledge or consent.
  • One of those networks, PXYEDGE, was identified as the rebranded successor to IpMoYu, a residential proxy service previously linked to BADBOX 2.0.
  • The researchers say PXYEDGE advertised approximately 200,000 proxy nodes, while their monitoring showed unique connections peaking at around 340,000.
  • HUMAN says some of the ad fraud traffic was also routed through these residential proxies to appear legitimate and evade anti-abuse filters.

⚙️ Key details

  • The infected devices fetch malware modules from public code repositories, while the same payloads are also mirrored across various hosting platforms for redundancy and to resist takedowns.
  • HUMAN says it also participated in Google’s disruption of the related XCPE malware operation earlier this month, which included taking down multiple C2 domains used by BADBOX 3.0.
  • Additionally, one of the malware repositories was taken down, while HUMAN says its systems now filter fraudulent advertising traffic associated with BADBOX 3.0.

item.title: Critical phpAfterShell Vulnerability Disclosed in PHP Session Handler
item.description:
Critical phpAfterShell Vulnerability Disclosed in PHP Session Handler

On November 19, 2026, the security research company depthfirst disclosed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), a critical vulnerability in PHP’s default file-based session handler that can lead to remote code execution. PHP released official patches to resolve this and 16 other security vulnerabilities on the same day. There is currently no indication that these vulnerabilities have been exploited in the wild.

🔍 Overview

Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, phpAfterShell scores a 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The PHP project addressed the flaw in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, and 8.6.0. These releases also resolve 16 other security vulnerabilities, six of which are similarly rated as critical.

As of November 19, 2026, none of the 17 vulnerabilities are listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and no reviewed sources report active exploitation.

🧩 How it works

PHP stores session data in files by default. The phpAfterShell vulnerability involves the session write and deserialization processes:

  • Session read: When an application calls session_start(), PHP reads the session file and deserializes its content into the $_SESSION array.
  • Session write: When the request ends, PHP writes the updated session back to the same file.
  • Interruption: phpAfterShell is triggered when this write operation is interrupted. Following an interruption, the session file can hold the beginning of the new session data followed by the leftover end of the old session data.
  • Deserialization: On the next request, session_start() deserializes this mixed content. If an attacker managed to shape the old session data, PHP can deserialize objects of the attacker’s choosing.

An attacker can shape the stored session data by using PHP’s session upload progress feature (which writes file upload progress into the session) or by targeting applications that store large user-controlled strings in the session. Although PHP notes that code execution requires a write interruption at a useful point and a suitable deserialization gadget chain in the application, depthfirst reports reaching code execution without any application gadget. They achieved this by chaining phpAfterShell with a second, undisclosed memory-corruption bug in a PHP-native class. It is unestablished whether this second bug is fixed in the November 19 releases.

⚙️ Mitigation and Protection

To mitigate the vulnerability, Cloudflare has updated its Web Application Firewall (WAF) to block known phpAfterShell attack patterns. These updates build on a PHP remote code execution rule first deployed in October 2026 for the php2shell vulnerabilities, which has now been updated to cover phpAfterShell.

Rule Name / Feature Target Vulnerability Managed Ruleset Default Action
phpAfterShell Rule CVE-2026-126714 Free and Paid (Enabled by default) Block
PHP-FPM Request Smuggling Rule CVE-2026-129289 Paid Plans (Enabled by default) Log
PHP SOAP Extension Rules CVE-2026-15353, CVE-2026-129506 Paid Plans (Enabled by default) Log

The request smuggling and SOAP rules use the “Log” action by default because the traffic patterns they target can occasionally occur in legitimate traffic. Paid plan customers can review matching requests in Security Events and change the action to “Block” once they verify that legitimate traffic is unaffected.

Cloudflare emphasizes that the WAF serves as an additional layer of defense rather than a complete replacement for patching. Because several of the critical flaws depend on server configuration or bypass pathways visible to the WAF, the only complete fix is to upgrade PHP and restart all worker processes.

#PHP #phpAfterShell #Cybersecurity #Cloudflare #Vulnerability
